result.summary: Æneas, driven by a storm back to Sicily, holds funeral games for Anchises, but Juno stirs the Trojan women to burn the fleet. After Jove's rain saves most ships, Æneas leaves the weary behind in a new city, Acesta, and sails on; Sleep drowns the helmsman Palinurus.

scenes.title: Storm drives fleet to Sicily
scenes.summary: Leaving Carthage, the Trojans meet a storm. Palinurus advises turning to Sicily, and Æneas agrees. Acestes welcomes them.
scenes.stakes: The fleet risks being lost in the storm and failing to reach Italy.

place.name: Sea toward Sicily and the Sicilian shore

scenes.title: Rites at Anchises' tomb
scenes.summary: Æneas announces games and offers sacrifice at his father's grave. A serpent emerges and tastes the offerings.
scenes.stakes: Honour owed to Anchises and the favour of the gods.

scenes.title: The ship race
scenes.summary: Four ships race round a rock. Gyas throws Menœtes overboard, Sergestus wrecks on the rocks, and Cloanthus wins with divine help.
scenes.stakes: Glory and prizes; Sergestus and Gyas lose through rage and haste.

scenes.title: The foot-race
scenes.summary: Nisus slips in blood but trips Salius so Euryalus wins. Æneas rewards Salius and Nisus fairly.
scenes.stakes: Prizes and honour for the runners.

scenes.title: Boxing: Dares and Entellus
scenes.summary: Dares challenges all; old Entellus is goaded by Acestes and beats him. Æneas halts the fight, and Entellus kills the bull for Eryx.
scenes.stakes: Entellus risks humiliation by age; Dares risks death.

scenes.title: Archery and the Trojan game
scenes.summary: Eurytion shoots the dove, Acestes' arrow bursts into flame as an omen, and the boys perform the Trojan cavalry game.
scenes.stakes: Prizes for archers; the omen foretells future events.

scenes.title: Juno incites the ship burning
scenes.summary: Iris, disguised as Beroe, rouses the Trojan women to burn the ships. Ascanius shames them; Æneas prays and Jove sends rain.
scenes.stakes: The whole fleet and the Trojans' hope of Italy.

place.name: Trojan camp on the Sicilian shore

scenes.title: Nautes' counsel; Anchises' vision
scenes.summary: Nautes advises leaving the weary behind; Anchises appears in a dream and urges Æneas to visit him in the underworld. Acesta is founded and the fleet departs.
scenes.stakes: Whether Æneas abandons Fate's call or fatally divides his people.

place.name: Trojan camp and new city, Sicily

scenes.title: Venus pleads with Neptune
scenes.summary: Venus begs Neptune for safe passage; he promises it at the cost of one life and calms the sea.

scenes.title: Death of Palinurus
scenes.summary: Sleep, disguised as Phorbas, drugs Palinurus and throws him overboard. Æneas steers the ship himself and mourns him.
scenes.stakes: Palinurus's life and the safety of the masterless ship.

place.name: Sea near the Sirens' isle
place.modern_name: Tyrrhenian Sea, off the Campanian coast

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for the Carthaginian queen.
Iris takes the shape of the old woman Beroe.
Sleep takes the likeness of Phorbas.
A name for the Trojans, after their ancestor Teucer.

notable_quotes.reason: Nautes' maxim that endurance conquers fortune.
Links the Trojan game to Roman tradition.

analysis.text: Games, grief and loss mark a pause in the journey: Æneas honours his father, yet Juno's wrath and Fate's price (Palinurus) remind him of the cost of destiny.
Virgil traces Roman families (Memmii, Sergii, Cluentii, Atii) and the Lusus Troiae to Trojan origins, flattering the Augustan aristocracy.

legacy.text: The funeral games of Anchises follow Homer's games for Patroclus and shaped later epic games, as in Statius' Thebaid.
The Lusus Troiae was revived by Julius Caesar and Augustus as a real Roman ceremony.

fun_facts.text: Dante echoes Palinurus' fate in the Purgatorio, where a soul recalls him.

language_notes.text: Elissa is another name for Dido, queen of Carthage, whom Æneas has just left. Her funeral flame is the pyre on which she killed herself.
"Outrage done on great love" means a betrayal of deep love. The Trojans guess Dido may have done something desperate, though they do not know the cause of the blaze.
"Shifts the sheet to the wind" means he trims the sail rope to catch the wind at a different angle.
Eryx was a son of Venus and so Æneas's half-brother, hence "brother-coast". Sicania is an old name for Sicily.
"Above ground" contrasts the living Acestes with Anchises, who is buried in Sicily. "Darden" means Trojan, from Dardanus.
Acestes was born in Sicily to a Trojan mother and the river-god Crimisus, which explains his Trojan kinship.
"Dardanus" was the legendary ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so "sons of Dardanus" means Trojans.
The Gætulian Syrtes (sandbanks off North Africa), the Argive main and Mycenæ name places of danger or enemy Greek territory, showing he would keep the rite anywhere.
"Gods of the hearth" are the household gods (Penates), honoured at meals and feasts.
"Teucrian" means Trojan, from the early king Teucer.
Myrtle was sacred to Venus, Æneas' mother, hence "his mother's myrtle".
"Whatever that name may import" is Æneas' wry aside: the Tiber's name means little to Anchises, who never reached it.
"Spires" and "volumes" both mean coils coiling of the serpent's body.
"Genius of the spot" is the guardian spirit of a place; Æneas wonders if the snake is that or Anchises' attendant.
Phaethon's steeds are the horses of the sun; the phrase means the sun-horses bringing in the ninth dawn after Anchises' burial rites began.
Guerdon means reward; chaplets are wreaths worn on the head; tripods are three-legged bronze vessels, valued as prizes.
Virgil traces Roman families (Memmii, Sergii, Cluentii) back to Trojan captains, flattering his Roman audience with legendary ancestors.
Gyas wants the helmsman to hug the turning post closely, keeping the rock on the left, which is the shorter, riskier route.
Mnestheus recalls earlier hard voyages: the Syrtes (African shoals), the Ionian Sea and Cape Malea (Greece's stormy southern cape) on the way from Troy.
Nereids are sea nymphs; Phorcus is an old sea god; Panopea is a Nereid; Portunus is a god of harbours.
The woven boy is Ganymede, carried off to serve the gods by Jove's eagle, the bearer of his thunderbolts.
Pallas' labours means weaving and handicrafts, the arts of Pallas Minerva.
Teucrian means Trojan, after the ancestor Teucer; Sicanian refers to the native people of Sicily, where the games are held.
Trinacrian means Sicilian; Trinacria was an old name for Sicily.
"Whom dim tradition leaves in darkness" means their names have been forgotten and are not recorded.
Unguerdoned means unrewarded; a guerdon is a reward or recompense.
Gnossian means from Gnossus (Knossos) in Crete, a place famed for archers and weapons.
Sliddery is an old form of slippery; ordure is dung or filth.
The shield was taken by the Greeks (Danaans) from a temple gate of Neptune, presumably at Troy; the maker Didymaon is otherwise unknown to most readers.
Fillet festoons: ribbons or woollen bands hung on sacrificial animals as decoration.
Thews means muscles or sinews, here suggesting great bodily strength.
Paris was Hector's brother and the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen began the war; Dares was his boxing champion. Butes and Amycus are earlier boxers; Amycus was a legendary Bebrycian king.
Goddess-born is a title for Æneas, whose mother was Venus.
Sons of Dardanus are the Trojans, descended from their ancestor Dardanus.
Eryx was a Sicilian king and boxer who taught Entellus; he was killed by Hercules in a bout. Trinacria is Sicily.
Hercules' gauntlets: Eryx once fought Hercules in a boxing match on this Sicilian shore, which Entellus recalls.
Alcides is another name for Hercules, from his grandfather Alceus.
Teucrian means Trojan; Trinacrian means Sicilian.
Entellus offers the bull's life in place of Dares' life, as a sacrifice to Eryx, his dead master.
The lots were drawn from a helmet; each archer's name was cast in, and the order of shooting was thereby decided.
Pandarus, in the Iliad (and Aeneid), broke the truce between Trojans and Greeks by shooting at Menelaus; Eurytion is his brother, so the Trojan archery lineage is recalled.
'Hapless man' addresses Mnestheus: his arrow missed the bird but cut its cord, freeing her.
Trinacria is Sicily; its people are Acestes' subjects, here watching alongside the Trojans.
'A prize drawn without a lot' means Acestes receives a prize by divine favour, not by placement in the contest.
Polites was a son of Priam killed at Troy; his son, named Priam, is here a boy leader. Italy's peopling alludes to his descendants.
The Atii were a Roman family, here flattered with a Trojan ancestor; Augustus's mother came from the Atii.
The labyrinth in Crete was built for the Minotaur; Theseus escaped it. It is compared to the riders' interweaving patterns.
This 'Game of Troy' (lusus Troiae) was a real Roman cavalry display by boys, performed in Virgil's day.
Juno's wrath against the Trojans began with the judgment of Paris and continued because Troy's descendants were fated to destroy her beloved Carthage.
Dardan means Trojan, after Dardanus, an ancestor of the Trojan kings. Teucrian in sentence 242 is another name for Trojans.
The seventh summer: the Trojans have wandered seven years since the fall of Troy. Retreating Italy means a land that keeps receding as they pursue it.
'Gainsay' means to oppose or contradict: who could forbid us to found a city here?
Xanthus and Simois are the rivers of Troy's plain; Hector was the Trojan champion killed by Achilles.
Cassandra was Priam's daughter, a prophetess doomed never to be believed. Here Juno uses her name to give false authority.
The four altars to Neptune are offered as a sign that the sea god himself supplies fire and approval.
'Exorcised' means driven out like an evil spirit, suggesting the women had been possessed by Juno's frenzy.
Tritonian Pallas is Minerva (Athena), called Tritonian from Lake Triton or the river Triton, a title linked to her birth or cult.
"Emprize" is an archaic word for an enterprise or daring undertaking; "timorsome" means fearful.
Dis is the king of the underworld (the Greek Pluto); Avernus is a lake near Cumae regarded as an entrance to the underworld.
The Sibyl is the prophetess of Cumae, who will guide Æneas in Book 6; black cattle are the customary offering to underworld powers.
"Daystar" is the morning star, here the sun's herald, whose horses' breath marks the approach of dawn, forcing the ghost to leave.
The "god of Pergamus" is Trojan household worship tied to Pergamus, Troy's citadel; Vesta is goddess of the hearth, whose shrine Æneas honors with meal and incense.
Eryx is the Sicilian mountain and its hero-god, linked to Æneas's half-brother, to whom sacrifice is owed. The entrails are thrown into the sea as a departure offering.
"Bespeaks" means addresses; "plaints" are complaints or laments; "fell" means cruel and fierce.
Phrygia stands for Troy and its people; the "remnants of Troy" are the Trojan survivors Æneas leads.
Refers to the storm in Book 1, when Juno bribed Æolus, keeper of the winds, to wreck Æneas' fleet off Libya.
Earlier in this book Juno sent Iris to incite the Trojan women, who burnt ships in Sicily; they were then left behind there.
Laurentian Tiber: the Tiber's mouth in Latium, near Laurentum, the Italian destination fated for the Trojans.
Venus was born from the sea, so Neptune says she has a right to trust his realms. Cythera was a island sacred to her.
Recalls Iliad events: Achilles slaughtered Trojans by the river Xanthus, and Neptune rescued Æneas from him in a cloud.
A hecatomb was a great sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen; here the slain Trojans are grimly called offerings to Death.
Avernus haven refers to the Italian coast near Lake Avernus at Cumae, the entrance to the underworld.
The one life is Palinurus the helmsman, who falls overboard later in this book.
"Sailyard's lofty horns" means the upper ends of the yard-arm, the horizontal spar that holds the sail; the crew trim the sails by hauling ropes on either side.
"Cope of heaven's arch" means the top of the vault of the sky; Night is near midnight.
Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld, and Styx is its river of oath and dread. Both lend the bough its power to drug.
Neptune had earlier promised Venus that the fleet would reach Italy safely; only one life would be lost.
The Sirens were creatures whose song lured sailors to wreck on their rocks; their shore is littered with bones.

context_notes.text: Palinurus is the fleet's helmsman. He is later lost overboard in Book 5.
Neptune is the Roman god of the sea, who controls waves and storms.
Anchises, Æneas's father, died and was buried in Sicily the year before, at Drepanum.
The games mark the anniversary of Anchises' death, who died in Sicily the previous year during the Trojans' journey.
Acestes is the Trojan-descended king of Sicily, who welcomed the fleet.
Libations of wine, milk and blood were standard offerings to the dead, believed to nourish their shades.
Snakes were often seen as embodiments of the dead or of guardian spirits at tombs.
Æneas is holding funeral games in Sicily, in honour of his father Anchises, who died a year earlier. Acestes is the local Trojan-descended king.
The oak marks the turning post; ancient boat races required ships to round a mark and return to the start.
Neptune is the god of the sea, so Mnestheus leaves the victory to his will.
The cuirass is a breastplate; its great weight shows the strength of its former owner, Demoleos.
Acestes is the Trojan-descended king of Sicily, who welcomes Æneas and hosts the funeral games for Anchises.
Olive wreaths were traditional victors' crowns in Greek-style athletic contests.
The blood is left from sacrifices made earlier at the games for the dead Anchises.
Boxing is one of the funeral games held in Sicily for Anchises, Æneas' father, on the anniversary of his death.
Gauntlets here are the caestus, a boxing glove of thongs of hide, sometimes weighted with metal.
Æneas, as host of the games, acts as judge and stops the fight.
A live dove tied to a mast is the target, a common archery contest in ancient epic.
Ascanius is also called Iulus; the Julian family, including Julius Caesar, claimed descent from him.
Dido, queen of Carthage, loved Aeneas and gave Ascanius (Iulus) gifts; she killed herself when Aeneas left, so this memento is poignant.
The games honour Anchises, Æneas' father, who died a year earlier in Sicily. 'Deified' reflects his heroic cult.
Iris is Juno's messenger and goddess of the rainbow, which is her path through the sky.
Pyrgo, Priam's old nurse, is the one woman who recognises the disguise, showing how the goddess is exposed.
Ascanius is Æneas' young son, also called Iulus, ancestor of the Julian family.
Acestes is a Sicilian king of Trojan descent, who has welcomed the Trojans. His mother was a Trojan woman, hence the mingled blood.
Jove sent rain to quench the fire set on the ships by the Trojan women, which is the rescue referred to.
Æneas founds the city by ploughing its boundary furrow, a Roman ritual custom, and assigns homes by lot.
Venus is Æneas' mother. Juno, queen of the gods, hates the Trojans and has persecuted them throughout the poem.
Neptune, son of Saturn and brother of Jove, rules the sea.
Neptune had built Troy's walls with Apollo, but Laomedon cheated them of payment; this is why he calls Troy perjured.
Sea deities such as Glaucus, Palæmon, Phorcus and the Nereids Thetis, Panopea and others form Neptune's retinue.
Palinurus is the fleet's helmsman; the other ships follow his lead at the head of the line.
Phorbas was a Trojan companion of Palinurus's family; Sleep takes his shape to win the helmsman's trust.

literary_notes.text: The Trojans' dark presage of what a desperate woman can do hints at Dido's suicide and the later hatred between Carthage and Rome.
The cloud "charged with night" and darkness that "ruffled" the waves treat the storm as an active, menacing force.
Fortune is imagined as a driver who pulls the reins, picturing fate as steering the fleet.
"Weeping" against "honour" shows the day's mixed grief and reverence.
Æneas addresses his dead father directly, and the words "rescued in vain" voice his sorrow.
The serpent's gleaming colours are compared to a rainbow, stressing its beauty and its marvellous, perhaps divine, quality.
"Two... two..." and "again and again" give the ritual a solemn, measured rhythm.
The speed of the ships is compared to chariots bursting from the starting gates, bringing a familiar land race to the sea.
The short sentences and present tense give the narration a breathless, commentator-like immediacy, as if the lead changes were seen live.
Gyas's fiery grief and his violent act reveal a proud, hot-tempered youth who puts winning above decency and safety.
The startled dove gliding smoothly captures Mnestheus's ship surging out of trouble into easy speed.
Cloanthus wins through divine aid after his vow; the sea gods push his ship, deciding the race.
The crushed serpent mirrors the wrecked Centaur dragging itself home, adding pathos and mockery to Sergestus's humiliation.
Nisus's speed is compared to wind and a winged thunderbolt, stressing how far he outpaces the field.
Calling Nisus "ill-starred" signals the coming fall, and hints at his later fate in Book 9.
The narrator's cry of "Poor youth!" shows direct sympathy and sets a tone of pathos.
Nisus sacrifices his own victory out of love for Euryalus, defining his devoted character.
Æneas, called "father", acts as a fair, compassionate leader, keeping the rules while showing pity.
Age is described as frost and ice, binding Entellus's limbs and expressing his lost vigor.
Dares probing Entellus's guard is compared to a general besieging a fortress, giving the boxing match the scale of war.
Entellus's heavy fall is likened to an uprooted pine crashing on a mountain, stressing his size and the weight of his failed blow.
The rain of blows is compared to hail rattling on a roof, conveying their speed and density.
The dove falling with the arrow in her breast is a vivid, almost pathetic picture.
The narrator hints that the omen's meaning only became clear later, probably the burning of the ships that follows.
The burning arrow is likened to shooting stars dragging 'blazing hair', making the omen visible and awe-inspiring.
The riders' intricate patterns are compared first to the Cretan labyrinth, then to dolphins at play, conveying both complexity and joy.
The passage explains the origin of a Roman custom, linking Troy to Rome and glorifying Roman tradition.
Fortune is treated as a being who changes allegiance, signalling a sudden turn from festive peace to disaster.
Juno is shown as cunning and practised in mischief, 'no novice in the ways of doing hurt'.
The fire is called a god who 'revels', making the blaze seem a living, gleeful power.
Fire is described as a creeping 'plague' that sinks into the ship's limbs, comparing the ship to a diseased body.
The storm answering Æneas' prayer shows Jove's favour returning and the Trojans' fate being preserved.
Anxiety is imagined as a heavy load he shifts from side to side, conveying his restless indecision.
Nautes' words are a kindling fire, so the advice inflames Æneas's anxiety rather than calming it.
Night is a black figure riding in a chariot across the sky, setting the scene for the dream apparition.
The vanishing ghost is compared to smoke dissolving into thin air, stressing its insubstantial nature.
Æneas addresses the departed ghost with urgent questions, expressing his longing to embrace his father.
Those who shrank from the sea now long to sail, reversing their earlier fear.
Venus presents herself as humbled, stressing Juno's relentless wrath to win sympathy and gain Neptune's help.
Confounding all ocean with heaven exaggerates the storm's scale to heighten Venus' complaint.
Neptune calls on the rivers Xanthus and Simois as witnesses, as if they could testify to his past care.
The promise of one life for thousands anticipates the death of Palinurus, casting a shadow over the safe passage.
The waves "sink down" and the sea "stills" as if obeying their master, showing Neptune's authority.
Night is dewy and Sleep a winged god who swims through the dark, turning natural drowsiness into a purposeful divine agent.
The narrator turns to address Palinurus directly ("in quest of you, poor Palinurus"), showing pity and foreshadowing his doom.
Palinurus's proud refusal to trust the calm sea is overturned moments later, and his warning about deceit proves true of Sleep himself.
Æneas's final words predict that Palinurus will lie unburied on an unknown shore, tying his death to his earlier trust in calm seas.
